strengths: Important and practical task: The paper addresses a highly relevant problem in autonomous driving, specifically the hybrid navigation challenge of associating online-perceived local HD maps with global SD maps.

Benchmark creation: The authors construct a large-scale dataset (OMA and OMA-GT) based on nuScenes and OpenStreetMap, featuring manual and automated alignment, which provides a valuable benchmark for the community.

Comprehensive evaluation metric: The proposed Association P-R metric considers both sequence alignment and length-aware overlaps, representing a more robust way to evaluate map association than simple Chamfer distance or KNN.

Strong and well-tailored baseline (MAT): The proposed Map Association Transformer incorporates path-aware attention for topological structures and spatial attention (via space-filling curve serialization and RoPE) for geometric coordinates.
Ablations and analysis: The paper includes thorough ablation studies analyzing different architecture choices, loss formulations (CE vs. CTC), and model scaling variants.
weaknesses: Limited comparisons with advanced methods: While map association is presented as a new benchmark, the baselines compared are only basic KNN and HMM. It would strengthen the paper to adapt other learning-based vector alignment or graph matching methods as additional baselines.

Unfair latency comparison: The latency of KNN and HMM is measured using unoptimized Python/NumPy implementations on CPU, whereas MAT is measured on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU. An optimized C++ version of HMM/KNN typically runs in sub-milliseconds, making the current comparison somewhat misleading.

Inconsistencies in training hyperparameters: There are some minor discrepancies in hyperparameter descriptions. For instance, Page 8 (Section 6.1) lists the learning rate as 0.0001, Table 9 lists it as 1e-5, and Section F.2 (Page 22) mentions a base learning rate of 2 * 10^-3 with a 10^-1 block-wise scaling factor.

Clarification on pipeline integration: The paper should clarify whether the map association framework (MAT) is trained/inferred entirely separate from the online map generation (MapTRv2) or if there is any joint training. It appears to be a two-stage pipeline, but a more explicit discussion of error propagation from the perception stage to the association stage is needed.

strengths: Clear and highly practical task formulation: Associating local, online-generated HD maps with global SD maps for hybrid navigation is an important, real-world challenge in autonomous driving.

Solid benchmark dataset: The proposed Online Map Association (OMA) dataset, built upon nuScenes and OpenStreetMap with manual annotations, provides a valuable resource for the autonomous driving research community.

Well-designed evaluation metric: The proposed Association Precision-Recall (Association P-R) metric is tailored to evaluate sequential and topological alignments rather than simple point-wise or chamfer-based matches, which better reflects downstream navigation needs.

Intuitive model design: The Map Association Transformer (MAT) leverages complementary spatial attention (SA) and path-aware attention (PA) to capture both geographic proximity and topological continuity.
weaknesses: Significant writing and compilation issues: The paper contains several incomplete sentences (e.g., the abstract ends abruptly with 'The code and dataset can be accessed at'). Additionally, the reference list is duplicated in the PDF (pages 10-11 and pages 12-14), which indicates a rushed and careless submission preparation.

Lack of modern learning-based baselines: The proposed MAT is only compared against very simple non-learning baselines (KNN and HMM). Comparing with or adapting other modern learning-based graph matching, cross-domain alignment, or standard transformer-based map matching methods would significantly strengthen the empirical evaluation.

Clarity on coordinate alignment: Since online HD maps are ego-centric and SD maps are global, more explicit details are needed in the main text regarding how they are pre-aligned (e.g., coordinate transformation, normalization) before vector tokens are extracted and fed into the transformer.

Unnecessary repetition in contributions: The introduction and abstract repeat the exact same set of contributions almost verbatim, while some variables in the formulation (such as Eq. 5) have minor typesetting issues (e.g., stray characters/superscripts near the closing parenthesis).

strengths: Practical Relevance: Associating local online HD maps with global SD maps is a highly relevant problem for hybrid navigation in autonomous driving, addressing a key limitation of modern online map construction models.

Benchmark Construction: The authors introduce OMA and OMA-GT datasets (derived from nuScenes and OpenStreetMap) with automated and manual refinement, providing a platform to study hybrid map association.

Custom Evaluation Metric: The proposed Association P-R metric improves upon Reachability P-R by incorporating sequence alignment and length-aware overlap checking, which is highly suited for structural matching.
Detailed Ablation Studies: The paper provides detailed ablation tables (Tables 3-5) evaluating the impact of different attention mechanisms, loss functions, and pooling techniques.
weaknesses: Severe Formatting and Bibliographical Errors: The bibliography is completely duplicated in the manuscript (pages 10-12 are repeated on pages 12-14), showing a lack of basic proofreading. Furthermore, the URL for the code and dataset in the abstract is left completely blank ("The code and dataset can be accessed at ").

Unfair and Misleading Latency Comparisons: In Table 1 and Table 2, the proposed MAT is shown to have lower latency than KNN and HMM. However, the authors state on page 9 that "the KNN and HMM code is developed using Python and Numpy without optimization". Comparing a deep Transformer on a GPU to unoptimized Python CPU code is misleading, as any standard C++ or vectorized implementation of KNN / HMM would take less than a millisecond.

Weak Baselines: The evaluation only compares MAT to extremely simple traditional methods (KNN and HMM). There are no comparisons to modern deep learning methods, graph matching architectures, or sequence-to-sequence map matching approaches.

Data Discrepancy in OMA: As shown in Table 6, the online HD map predictions in OMA are highly noisy, with the average lane count per scene being 310.34 compared to 78.6 in OMA-GT, indicating extreme over-segmentation and false positives. If the input online perception is this degraded, the practicality of downstream association remains questionable.

Limited Technical Novelty: The components of MAT are largely derivative, combining path-aware attention (adapted from MapTRv2), spatial serialization attention (inspired by PTv3), and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) from existing LLMs/VLMs.

strengths: Practical and highly relevant task definition: Online Navigation Refinement (ONR) effectively bridges the gap between global, cheap, but coarse SD maps and local, real-time, but topology-free online perception (OP) maps, presenting a low-cost alternative to expensive global HD maps.

First-of-its-kind benchmark: The paper introduces the Online Map Association (OMA) dataset, containing over 30K scenarios and 2.6M manually annotated lane vectors, which serves as a valuable resource for the autonomous driving and GIS community.

Efficient and elegant method design: The Map Association Transformer (MAT) incorporates Path-Aware Attention (topology grouping) and Spatial Attention (vector serialization using space-filling curves) to reduce attention complexity from quadratic to linear, achieving a real-time latency of 34 ms.

Extensive and convincing evaluation: The authors validate their method against a wide range of baselines (HMM, deep map matching, graph/point matching) and across three different upstream perception map generators (MapTR, MapTRv2, SeqGrowGraph). Excellent robustness tests are also conducted under imperfect SD maps and environmental corruptions (nuScenes-C).
weaknesses: Geographic and structural scope limits: The benchmark is built solely on the Boston and Singapore segments of nuScenes. While the cross-city generalization is verified, the geographic and structural variety remains somewhat limited to these regions.

Downstream performance bottleneck: There is a notable drop in association performance when transitioning from the ground-truth OP maps in the validation set (NR-F1 ~78%) to the noisy, generated OP maps in the test set (NR-F1 ~41-55%). This highlights that the system is strongly bottlenecked by the quality of upstream perception.

Clarity on intersection/transition areas: The multi-to-one classification formulation (mapping each lane/centerline to a single road class) can become ambiguous at intersection zones where lanes merge, split, or cross. While transition handling is briefly discussed in Appendix D.6, a more detailed architectural discussion on how the model handles multi-labeled transition segments in the main text would improve clarity.

strengths: Introduces a highly practical and novel task, Online Navigation Refinement (ONR), which bridges the gap between road-level navigation from SD maps and local metric lanes from online perception (OP) maps, bypassing the high cost of global HD maps.

Presents the Online Map Association (OMA) dataset, a large-scale, manually annotated benchmark with over 30K scenarios and 2.6M annotated lane vectors, which represents a significant resource contribution to the community.

The proposed Map Association Transformer (MAT) incorporates well-motivated structural designs tailored for spatial-topological data: Path-Aware Attention to enforce topological alignment and Spatial Attention using space-filling curves (e.g., Hilbert curves) for geometric clustering.
Establishes a dedicated evaluation metric, Navigation Refinement P-R (NR P-R), which accounts for noisy predicted maps and penalizes fragmentation and topological errors.

Provides extensive experimental validation, including zero-shot robustness tests on environmental corruptions (using nuScenes-C), imperfect SD maps with noise, and multiple upstream OP map generators, demonstrating impressive performance and real-time efficiency (34 ms latency).
weaknesses: The technical components, such as token serialization using space-filling curves and group-based local attention, are conceptually similar to techniques used in 3D point cloud processing and linear transformers. The novelty of these individual operators is somewhat incremental, though their fusion for map association is effective.

The map-matching baselines (e.g., HMM, DeepMM, EAM3) are inherently designed for trajectory-to-map matching. While the authors' workaround of converting OP paths to trajectories is logical, these baselines may not be optimized for handling the structural properties of map-to-map alignment.

Since the OMA dataset is derived from nuScenes, it inherits a geographic focus on urban areas in Boston and Singapore. Evaluation on more diverse layouts, such as complex highway interchanges or rural environments, would further strengthen the claims of generalizability.

strengths: Practical and Crucial Task Definition: The introduction of the Online Navigation Refinement (ONR) task is highly relevant and timely. Leveraging cheap, global SD maps for routing and combining them with real-time online perception maps is a very promising alternative to cost-prohibitive, globally-maintained HD maps.

Comprehensive Dataset Contribution: The creation and release of the Online Map Association Dataset (OMA) with over 30K scenarios and 2.6M annotated lane vectors provides a much-needed benchmark to push research in this specific sub-field forward.

Novel Attention Mechanisms: The design of Path-Aware Attention (topological ordering) and Spatial Attention (space-filling curves) is a clever way to handle structural and spatial heterogeneity under linear complexity constraints, resulting in low latency (34 ms).

Extensive Evaluation and Robustness Analyses: The authors provide highly detailed evaluations, including zero-shot generalization on environmental corruptions (nuScenes-C), robustness to noisy/imperfect SD maps (shifts, omissions, noise), and testing across different upstream map generators (MapTR, MapTRv2, SeqGrowGraph).
weaknesses: High Sensitivity to Upstream Failures: The proposed map association relies entirely on the quality of online perception (OP) maps. If the upstream perception network fails to detect critical lanes or produces highly distorted geometries (e.g., in highly complex or unstructured intersections), the downstream association may suffer from severe cascade errors. A more detailed quantitative study on how association accuracy degrades relative to upstream map generation quality (e.g., mAP) would strengthen the paper.

Potential Unfairness in Baseline Adaptations: Several baseline methods (e.g., HMM, DeepMM, MTrajRec) were originally engineered for trajectory-to-map matching (GPS trajectories to road networks). Although the authors adapt them for map-to-map matching, these algorithms may not perform optimally under this modified formulation, making the comparison slightly less direct.

Limited Geographical and Structural Diversity: Since the benchmark is built upon nuScenes data, it is geographically restricted to Boston and Singapore. Autonomous driving models often face domain generalization issues when transferred to different road layouts, such as complex European roundabouts or massive multi-level flyovers in Asian megacities. The generalization capability of the model on globally diverse road networks is not fully proven.

Cluttered Presentation and Dense Notation: The manuscript packs a very high volume of information, which occasionally impacts readability. The mathematical formulation in Section 5.1 is somewhat dense, and some notations could be simplified. Refining the prose and streamlining the equations would make the methodology more accessible.
